# Introduction {#sec-introduction}

This document proposes an improved template algorithm in Actual Budget (@fig-algorithm-diagram). The template algorithm is what runs whenever you click "Apply budget template" or "Overwrite with budget template" in Actual Budget. The proposed algorithm primarily changes the way long-term templates (e.g., `by`-type templates) are handled to make the monthly contributions more consistent and manageable when there are multiple long-term templates in the budget file.

## Background

In Actual Budget, [templates](https://actualbudget.org/docs/experimental/goal-templates) are tools to automate your contributions to spending categories each month. Most are pretty straightforward. For example, `#template 50` will budget \$50 in a category each month, and `#template average 12 months` will budget equal to a category's average spending over the previous 12 months. Both of these examples, like most templates, prescribe a specific amount to be budgeted. But there are other templates that work differently. The template `#template 500 by 2027-02` will aim to build up a \$500 balance in the category by February of 2027. The template `#template schedule Car Insurance` will work similarly, but will take its amount and date from an upcoming scheduled transaction called "Car Insurance."

The most intuitive way to save up for a future expense is to calculate how much you will need to save monthly at the start, then save that much each month. We'll call this the *naïve* method.^["Naïve" here is used in the academic sense---the simplest, most obvious approach.]

$$ \text{contribution} = \frac{\text{goal} - \text{starting balance}}{\text{goal month} - \text{starting month} + 1} $$ {#eq-naive} 

However @eq-naive requires storing the starting date and starting balance of a savings goal, or storing the monthly contribution amount once initially calculated. Actual Budget doesn't store this information, so the amount to contribute must be calculated based on the *current* month and *current* balance only. For a single long-term template, we can use a "memoryless" version (@eq-memoryless) instead.

$$ \text{contribution} = \frac{\text{goal} - \text{\textit{current} balance}}{\text{goal month} - \text{\textit{current} month} + 1} $$ {#eq-memoryless} 

The memoryless version does have some advantages, namely, if you unexpectedly spend from or contribute to the category you're saving in, the memoryless approach will automatically adjust your future contributions to still meet the goal. And if nothing like that happens, the memoryless version will behave exactly like the naïve version. However, if there multiple long-term goals simultaneously, the memoryless approach becomes harder to manage. It's difficult to know exactly how much to save in any month without remembering the starting dates of specific goals.

Complex combinations of templates, including mixing several long-term `by` or `schedule` templates, do happen in regularly. In my life this is my pet expenses category. There are regular monthly expenses such as food, plus several larger expenses I want to save up for: a yearly vet visit in January, a yearly purchase of heartworm preventative chews in March, and occasionally, one-off boarding expenses for upcoming travel.

![Maisie, enjoying a purchase from the 'Maisie' category.](img/maisie.jpg)

Other people may experience this in a category for bills. In addition to monthly bills, they may want to save up for car insurance every 6 months and renters insurance every year, two longer term goals of different frequencies and different amounts.

## The Problem: Current Actual Budget Behavior

When you put multiple long-term goals into one category, the resulting behavior in Actual Budget is a bit weird. Consider @exm-multiple-by.

::: {#exm-multiple-by}

*Multiple `by`-type templates.*

It's the beginning of April of 2026. You have a \$100 balance in a spending category carried over from March. There are three upcoming expenses in that category you want to save up for:

- In July, you need to pay \$300.
- In August, you need to pay \$400.
- In October, you need to pay \$100.

To prepare for these expenses, you add the following three templates to the category:

```
#template 300 by 2026-07
#template 400 by 2026-08
#template 100 by 2026-10
```

:::

With these three templates, @tbl-actual-current shows what happens over the next 7 months.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-actual-current
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "The results of having the three 'by' templates in a single category as of Actual Budget v26.9.0."

startmonth = YearMonth(2026,4)
startbalance = 100

current = pd.DataFrame(
    {"Month":[startmonth + i for i in range(7)],
    "Budgeted":[144.29, 135.24, 113.57, 31.90, 208.33, 33.34, 33.33],
    "Spent":[0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 300.0, 400.0, 0.0, 100.0]}
)
current["Balance"] = (current["Budgeted"] - current["Spent"]).cumsum() + startbalance

Markdown(tabulate(current, headers="keys", showindex=False, floatfmt=".2f"))
```

This works, in the sense that the total contributed amount over 7 months is $700 (the total of all goals minus the initial balance) and the category balance is never overdrawn. But he contribution amounts are inconsistent and counterintuitive month-to-month.

If we were able to use the naïve method in this case by keeping track of goal start dates, @tbl-naive shows how much we would contribute and spend in each month.


```{python}
#| label: tbl-naive
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "The results of using the naïve amount divided by time algorithm to save for the three upcoming expenses."

startmonth = YearMonth(2026,4)
startbalance = 100

save_goal1 = (300 - startbalance) / 4
save_goal2 = 400 / 5
save_goal3 = 100 / 7

naive = pd.DataFrame(
    {"Month":[startmonth + i for i in range(7)],
    "Budgeted":[
        save_goal1+save_goal2+save_goal3, 
        save_goal1+save_goal2+save_goal3, 
        save_goal1+save_goal2+save_goal3,  
        save_goal1+save_goal2+save_goal3, 
        save_goal2+save_goal3, 
        save_goal3, 
        save_goal3],
    "Spent":[0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 300.0, 400.0, 0.0, 100.0]}
)
naive["Balance"] = (naive["Budgeted"] - naive["Spent"]).cumsum() + startbalance

Markdown(tabulate(naive, headers="keys", showindex=False, floatfmt=".2f"))
```

The values in this table result from counting the 100 already in the category towards the first goal and saving `{python} format(save_goal1, ".2f")` per month for the first goal, `{python} format(save_goal2, ".2f")` per month for the second goal, and `{python} format(save_goal3, ".2f")` per month for the third goal. These values are generally more intuitive for people -- more money is put aside each month initially, then less as each goal passes. And I think they are preferred by people because they are more consistent month-to-month and avoid sudden large contributions in a month.

Behavior similar to the naïve algorithm can be forced in Actual Budget by simply splitting long-term savings goals into their own categories. But this doesn't always make sense for people's budgets. For example, I don't want to have a separate category for vet, heartworm pills, dog food, and dog boarding. I just want one "Maisie" category.

## The Solution: A Better Template Algorithm

A template algorithm exists that is better than both the current Actual Budget algorithm *and* the naïve method. @tbl-better shows a series of contributions for @exm-multiple-by that meets all of the requirements (\$700 total contributed and balance is never negative), but with some distinct advantages.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-better
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "A series of contributions that meets all three spending goals while being more consistent than either the default Actual Budget behavior or the naïve algorithm."

startmonth = YearMonth(2026,4)
startbalance = 100

better = pd.DataFrame(
    {"Month":[startmonth + i for i in range(7)],
    "Budgeted":[0.0] * 7,
    "Spent":[0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 300.0, 400.0, 0.0, 100.0],
    "Balance": [0.0] * 7}
)

goals = [
    GradualGoal(YearMonth(2026,7), 300, "spending"),
    GradualGoal(YearMonth(2026,8), 400, "spending"),
    GradualGoal(YearMonth(2026,10), 100, "spending")
]

balance = startbalance
for i in range(better.shape[0]):
    month = better.loc[i,"Month"]
    contrib = contribution_amounts(
        [g for g in goals if g.month >= month], 
        [], 
        month, 
        {"spending":balance},
        []
    )[0]["spending"]
    better.loc[i,"Budgeted"] = contrib
    balance += contrib - better.loc[i,"Spent"]
    better.loc[i,"Balance"] = balance


Markdown(tabulate(better, headers="keys", showindex=False, floatfmt=".2f"))

```

The maximum amount contributed in any month is only `{python} format(max(better["Budgeted"]), ".2f")` in this scenario, compared to `{python} format(max(naive["Budgeted"]), ".2f")` in the naïve method and `{python} format(max(current["Budgeted"]), ".2f")` in the current version of Actual Budget. The contribution amount is also consistent for more consecutive months than in either other method. These advantages are shown more clearly in @fig-contributions.

```{python}
#| label: fig-contributions
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Contribution amounts per month for each algorithm from 2026-04 to 2026-10. The current Actual Budget algorithm results in erratic contribution amounts. The naïve algorithm is better in that regard, but the proposed algorithm has the most consistent contribution amounts and the smallest maximum contribution amount required to meet all three goals.

series = pd.DataFrame(
    {"Current": current["Budgeted"],
    "Naïve": naive["Budgeted"],
    "Proposed": better["Budgeted"]}
)
labels = better["Month"]

with plt.style.context("ggplot"):
    plt.grouped_bar(series, tick_labels=labels, colors=["purple", "blue", "green"])
    plt.legend(loc="upper right")
    plt.title("Monthly Contributions for Each Algorithm")
plt.show()
```

This series of contributions is produced by the algorithm proposed in the rest of this document. This algorithm is compatible with the existing template algorithm in two key ways:

1. It tries to match the behavior of the existing template algorithm in all scenarios except when there are multiple long-term templates in one budget file.
2. It maintains the memorylessness of Actual Budget templates, and requires no new information to be stored in the database.

But it also makes several improvements:

1. The maximum amount required to be withdrawn from available funds over the lifetime of the templates is lower than in any other algorithm.
2. The algorithm allows for `by`-type templates in the same category to have different priorities.
3. The algorithm is extendable to template types that may be added in the future.
